newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Secret mass graves haunt Nicaraguan elections.
newsitem.headline: Secret mass graves haunt Nicaraguan elections.

text.p: The victims may have died quietly with a bullet to the head but now the mass graves have become a big issue in the nation's presidential election.

Top candidates from left and right are blaming each other after the discovery of clandestine graves filled with bodies from the civil war in the 1980s. Right-wing politicians charge that the bodies are those of men executed by the left-wing Sandinista revolutionaries after they seized power in 1979.

The Sandinistas, whose candidate, former President Daniel Ortega, is running second in opinion polls, say they have evidence that 862 people were executed by the right-wing Contra forces during the civil war.

Impartial figures on the number of dead from both sides are hard to come by. Unlike its Central American neighbour El Salvador, Nicaragua never formed an independent commission to investigate human rights abuses after the war ended in 1990.

Estimates of the number of people who disappeared vary and the majority of the mass graves left by Sandinista security forces and U.S.-backed Contra rebels between 1979 and 1990 have not been exhumed, Lino Hernandez, president of Nicaragua's Permanent Centre for Human Rights (CPDH), said.

Now the long-dormant issue has burst onto the electoral agenda after a secret grave containing seven bodies was discovered on Aug. 15, Hernandez said. The victims were allegedly executed by triumphant Sandinista forces after the 1979 revolution that toppled dictator Anastasio Somoza.

The impact of the discovery, largely ignored by the Sandinista-controlled media, has snowballed as conservative newspaper La Prensa has run a series of articles on human rights abuses during the Sandinista regime that governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990, fighting an eight-year civil war against right-wing Contra rebels that left 30,000 dead.
"Unfortunately for the Sandinistas it has put the issue of mass graves on the election agenda. One party's dirty laundry is an election resource for their rivals," Hernandez said.

The reports of Sandinista human rights abuses came as the party was surging in the polls for the October election. The timing of the discovery and La Prensa's coverage led Ortega to accuse the newspaper of running a "dirty campaign" against his party in what has become an increasingly negative election.
"What would happen if we started releasing information on mass graves left by Somoza's genocidal National Guard?" the former president asked reporters.
Ortega has tried to equate the front-runner in the polls, conservative Arnoldo Aleman, with the Somoza family, which ruled Nicaragua with an iron fist for 43 years.
